en: The Sutra on the Original Causes for the Rebirth in the Pure Land of Avalokiteśvara Bodhisattva.
Translator lost; now appended to the Western Jin Record.
Thus have I heard: At one time, the Buddha was staying at Vulture Peak Mountain in the city of Rājagṛha, together with a great assembly of bhikṣus.

Surrounded by and revered by the great bodhisattvas, the devas, nāgas, the eight classes of beings, humans, and non-humans, he spoke of the causal origins of the great bodhisattvas' past lives (*jātaka*).
At that time, a great radiance appeared before the Buddha, illuminating all of Jambudvīpa in the south, gradually reaching other lands and realms. Within that radiance, a verse was spoken:

Having accomplished the liberation door of great compassion, he constantly dwells on Mount Potalaka in this Sahā world, observing the world six times throughout the day and night. Through the causal conditions of his original vow, he benefits all beings.
At that time, the assembly beheld this radiance and heard the recitation of these verses; they conceived a sense of the unprecedented, and there was none who did not feel doubt.

It was strange. When he questioned them in succession regarding the causes and conditions, there was no one who could answer. At that time, among the assembly, there was a bodhisattva mahāsattva named Dhāraṇīśvara.
Rising from his seat, he addressed the Buddha, saying: "World-Honored One, what are the causes and conditions [for this]?"
This radiance has appeared. Who has emitted it? We, this great assembly, having seen this light and heard these verses being recited, do not yet know the causes and conditions.
We pray that you will explain the causes and conditions for our sake. The Buddha addressed the Bodhisattva Sovereign of Dharani:
"Excellent, excellent! Listen attentively. From here, to the west, passing through buddha-fields as numerous as the sands of twenty Ganges Rivers..."
There is a world named Sukhāvatī. The sentient beings in that land have no manifold sufferings; they experience only various forms of bliss.
In that country there is a Buddha named Amitābha, filled with the noble assembly of the three vehicles.
Among them is a Great Being in his last birth before Buddhahood, named Avalokiteśvara, who has long planted roots of goodness and perfected the practices and vows of great compassion. Now...
He has come to this land desiring to reveal the fundamental causes and conditions for rebirth in the Pure Land; therefore, he has manifested this radiance that universally illumines the world.
Before long, he will come of his own accord. You all should inquire about the causes and conditions of these verses.

At that time, the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Avalokiteśvara, together with a multitude of hundreds of thousands of great bodhisattvas, came together to the summit of Vulture Peak and bowed their heads [in prostration].

Having paid homage to the Buddha, offered praises and offerings, and withdrawn to sit at one side, the Bodhisattva Sovereign of Total Retention (Dhāraṇī-vaśitā), empowered by the Buddha’s majesty, went to where Avalokiteśvara was, exchanged greetings with him, and addressed Avalokiteśvara, saying:

"O son of good family, regarding the light you have emitted and the subtle verses you have recited, we do not yet know their origin or the causes and conditions behind them; what is your intention? At that time...
Avalokiteśvara addressed Dhāraṇī-vaśitā, saying: "In the distant past, incalculable asaṃkhyeya kalpas ago, there was a country in Southern Jambudvīpa named Maṇipāṭa.
In that country lived a brahmin named Dīrghanakha, whose household was wealthy and prosperous. He had a wife named Maṇasrā, but they had no son."
Śikṣita. The husband and wife were constantly sighing in regret: "Although our wealth and property are abundant, we have no other concern;
yet, the fact that we have no offspring remains a source of deep resentment. They prayed to the heavenly deities, earnestly seeking a son.

Before long, his wife became pregnant, and when her months were full, she gave birth to a boy who was peerlessly handsome. When he reached the age of three, another son was born. [He was named] Brahmadatta.

They obtained two sons and were filled with joy and exultation. They summoned a physiognomist to examine the two boys. Upon seeing them, the physiognomist was not pleased and, after a long while, declared:

"Although these children are handsome, they will soon be separated from their parents. He named the elder brother *Prāgeva-viyoga* (Early Separation) and the younger brother *Kṣipra-viyoga* (Swift Separation).
Despite hearing these words, the husband and wife continued to cherish and nourish them without weariness. When Early Separation reached the age of seven...
In the fifth year [after his birth], his mother, Mānasarā, suddenly fell gravely ill due to a disorder of the four elements.
Her physical appearance deteriorated, and she suffered from the afflictions of a painful illness, unable to lie down in peace.

As her intake of water and food ceased and she entered the gateway of death, her two sons remained at her side, gazing up at her face while weeping in sorrow and grief. When the elder son heard his mother’s lamentation...
With tears mingling with blood, he rose from his sickbed and, rubbing the heads of his two sons with both hands, said:
"Birth, death, decay, and ruin cannot be avoided or escaped. What the diviners and physiognomists have foretold is indeed true.

It is my regret that you have not yet reached the prime of your youth when I must abandon you and part from you. What sin have I committed to receive such retribution? Why do you lack good fortune? At that time, early...
Leaving him by his pillow, she lay there in a swoon. After a long while, she revived and rose; calling out to heaven, she cried:
"We are now but children, ignorant and without understanding. If not our biological mother, who would have shown us the path of clear conduct?

Heaven and earth are vast and empty; the spirit has no refuge. Why this abandonment and parting? Her compassionate mother then exhorted her, saying: "It is the natural law of the world that those who are born..."
It must surely perish; like a swift current, it will certainly not remain for long. Now, hearing this mournful sound, I feel deep sorrow and regret.
Furthermore, quickly casting aside your youthful mind, stretch out both hands, tighten your slender neck, and wail aloud with a loud cry.
At that time, Maṇasara said to his two sons: "In the practice of the supreme Way, nothing surpasses the arousal of the bodhicitta. As for the bodhicitta—"
This is great compassion. When one reaches old age and wishes to repay the four debts of gratitude, it is fitting to resolve the mind [to practice].
Just as now, do not weep; although I am dying, you shall dwell with your father. Then he called Longna and spoke these final words:
"I have now given you two sons, like the wheels of a chariot or the wings of a bird. I die and you live; you must love and nourish them."
"It is no different from when I was born; do not let your heart change because of external circumstances. When the Brahmin heard his wife’s final words, he fainted and collapsed on the ground.
Upon regaining consciousness, he cried out: "A chariot with but one wheel does not advance even an inch; a bird with but one wing does not fly even a foot through the air.
You have entered the gate of death; with whom shall I raise our two children? Husband and wife are now parted—what a tragedy!"
Her love reached the point of sorrow. "I take no pleasure in this world; I am about to give up my life and enter the gate of death.
At that time, the wife spoke again: "These two sons were born to you and me together. I pray that you will stop this separation and nourish them. Having finished speaking, she closed her eyes.
The father and the two sons took her final words, buried the corpse, and returned home. The elder brother sat upon his father’s right knee, longing for his mother; the younger son sat on the left.
Upon his left knee, seeking food, he was filled with grief. Within his sorrowful heart, the brahmin thought to himself:
"I have no power to seek another woman as a wife to raise my young child. At that time, there was a brahmin named Vīra who had a daughter whose character was pure and virtuous.
He immediately took her and accepted her as his wife. At that time, the whole world suffered from the misery of famine, and wealth and grain were gradually exhausted in the storehouses.
They were destitute and had no means of livelihood. Changna then said to his wife, "I have heard that seven days' journey to the north lies Mount Tāla, where there is a sweet fruit called tinduka.
I shall go to that mountain to gather these excellent fruits so that I may support you and our two children.
While you and I are away, they will be able to be nourished. His wife accepted his words and cared for the two children.
"Son, like a biological mother. After Fu Chai had gone alone to that mountain, twenty-one days passed and he did not return.
At that time, his wife conceived a strange thought and reflected thus: "If Changna does not return from staying on that mountain, how shall I nourish and raise my two children?
Even if he returns to gather fruit, since he is so devotedly fond of the two children, what share will I have? Now..."
Using skillful means, he dismissed his two sons. Having reflected thus, he spoke to the sea captain: "The time for our certain departure has arrived.
He further addressed his two sons: "I lack the strength to support you. Since your father has not yet returned, there is an island nearby to the south, situated in isolation by the seashore.
On its shores are sweet fruits, and along the beach is fine grass. I shall go with you all to that isolated island. Thus he spoke.
They went to the boatman’s place. The two sons both boarded the boat and crossed the sea, arriving at the shore of a remote island.

He said to the two sons, "You two go down first and play on the beach, tossing about the sand. I shall remain in the boat to manage the remaining provisions; you may come down next when you wish to seek grass and fruit.
The two sons immediately disembarked and ran about here and there, playing and unaware of anything else. Thereafter, the stepmother secretly boarded [the boat].
The ship returned to their native land. When the two sons reached their own shore, they saw that the vessel was gone; they did not know where their mother had gone.
Exhausted from running along the seashore, they raised their voices and called out for her, but there was no answer. For day and night the two brothers wept in sorrow. The elder brother said:
"Our grieving mother bid us farewell and departed; once gone, she has not returned. Our compassionate father went to offer alms."
On Mount Nara, he did not return again. His stepmother placed him on a remote island and secretly departed. How could he sustain his life?
At that time, he recalled the words left behind by his birth mother: "I must resolve to attain the unsurpassed mind of enlightenment;

I shall perfect the great compassion of a bodhisattva and practice the gates of liberation. I must first deliver others, and only then attain Buddhahood. If there were no parents, [how would this have been possible?]"

To those who are parents, he manifests the form of parents; to those who are elders without a teacher, he manifests the body of a teacher; to those who are poor and lowly, he manifests the body of one who is wealthy and noble;
and to kings, ministers, elders, householders, officials, brahmins, and the fourfold assembly and the eight classes of beings, he likewise manifests their respective forms.
He manifests in every form for all beings; may I always remain on this island and be able to bestow peace and happiness upon the lands of the ten directions.
May I transform myself into mountains, rivers, the great earth, grasses, trees, the five grains, sweet fruits, and so forth, so that those who enjoy them may quickly transcend birth and death.
May I follow my mother wherever she is born, never departing from the place where my father is born. Thus he made one hundred such vows.
His life came to an end. His father, Dīrghanakha, having gathered *cintāmaṇi* fruits from Mount Tānula and returning to his home, first asked about his two sons.
His stepmother immediately replied, "Your sons are currently out wandering, begging for food and drink.
His father had a friend to whom he went and asked where his sons were. That friend replied, "After you left, two weeks have passed."
The stepmother sent her away to a remote island in the South Sea; she will surely starve to death, there is no doubt.
At that time, Dīrghanakha cried out, deeply reproaching himself: "I went to Mount Tāṇḍula to fetch sweet fruits for the sake of nourishing my two children;

what crime have I committed? Suddenly I have encountered this sorrow of separation from them. Previously, the hardship of parting was difficult to bear; now I have also met with the separation of death."
He immediately sought out a small boat and reached the shore of a remote island. Searching in all directions, he found nothing but a heap of white bones gathered in one place;
the clothes were scattered along the seashore. Knowing these to be the remains of his son’s death, he took the clothes and the bones and wept as he made this vow:
"May I deliver all suffering sentient beings and quickly attain the Buddha-way. May I transform the great earth, or [control] water and fire."
As wind, he may transform grasses, trees, and forests to serve as a refuge for sentient beings; or he may transform the five grains to augment the bodies of others;
or, whether as devas, humans, or spirits, he manifests his form in every land, among all classes—high and low—and in every variety of appearance and color.
Thus he made five hundred vows. Furthermore, he vowed: "May I always dwell in this Sahā world, preaching the Dharma and transforming sentient beings.
Until such a time as my life ends without food, may the Jambudvīpa tremble greatly, the devas assemble, and the birds and beasts cry out in sorrow and unease.
May my skeletal remains be scattered and transformed in the air as an offering. At that time, the Brahmin Daṇḍa was none other than the present Śākyamuni.
The Muni Tathāgata is he. His mother, Maṇasrā, is the Western Tathāgata Amitābha.
The elder brother, Zao-li, is my own self. The younger brother, Su-li, is the Bodhisattva Mahāsthāmaprāpta.
As for the friend, he is the Bodhisattva Samantabhadra. The mountain formerly known as Mount Dānala is now Mount Gṛdhrakūṭa (Vulture Peak).
The former isolated island is now Mount Potalaka. At the time when the kalpa is destroyed, although the physical world is ruined, when the kalpa is formed, its former signs reappear.
On the northern face of that mountain there is a hollow, within which lies a great boulder like a vajra.
It is named Ratnakarman. I have always been upon that stone, preaching the gate of liberation through the practice of great compassion to bring sentient beings to fulfillment.
Because I made a vow there in the past when I first departed from home, there stands atop the mountain a palace of the seven treasures, wondrously adorned and magnificent.

I am always within that precious palace, teaching, instructing, benefiting, and gladdening others. This was the place where I called out to my parents in the past; I rely upon that memory to go there.
Having been born in the Pure Land, they attained the stage of non-retrogression. Because they recalled their former self-sacrifice, they always remained upon that mountain.
Various species of birds and beasts, whom I had previously transformed, manifested as grasses and trees, bowing their leaves toward the place where the body was sacrificed.
You should know that the verses within the radiance are likewise so; such are the causal conditions from beginning to end. At that time, the Tathāgata Śākyamuni praised Avalokiteśvara.
"Avalokiteśvara Bodhisattva, excellent, excellent! It is truly as you have said. The causes and conditions for rebirth are each exactly like this.
You should know that today marks the beginning and end of the single transformation of myself and Amitābha. It is, for example, like a parent who has an only son;
when the child falls into the bottom of a well during a calamity, the father enters the bottom of the well to rescue his son and place him on the bank."

Above, his mother stands on the shore, embracing and nurturing him; his kinsmen assist the mother in her resolve to raise him, establishing the proper etiquette for friends so that he shall not return to the filth within the well.
I am like the compassionate father; sentient beings in the five turbidities are like those following at the bottom of the well;
Amitābha is like the merciful mother standing upon the shore; and Avalokiteśvara and others of the Pure Land are like friends, enabling one to attain non-retrogression.

Just as with those who are non-returners (*anāgāmin*), one should know that they enter into the five turbidities and defilements of this Sahā world to teach and transform the ignorant sentient beings of the six realms.
Having now been born in the Pure Land, Amitābha Buddha does not abandon them; Avalokiteśvara and Mahāsthāmaprāpta protect them, ensuring they do not fall back.
All of this is due to the causes and conditions of their past vows. At that time, the Tathāgata Amitābha, [accompanied by] countless hundreds...
A thousand holy beings appeared in the sky and spoke these verses:
“Excellent, Śākyamuni! Amidst the turbidity, you benefit sentient beings; Those who hear your name or behold your form Are certain to attain the path of Buddhahood.
Due to causes and conditions from the past, You have now come to appear in the sky.”
If you wish to be born in my land, you must surely come to welcome me in the West.
At that time, Śākyamuni Buddha praised Amitābha, speaking in verse:
“Excellent, O Honored One among Two-Legged Beings! You are able to benefit the Sahā world; You bear witness to the true Dharma.”

Out of compassion, he bestows all things; Even those with heavy karmic obstructions, By relying on the power of Amitābha’s vow as the cause for birth in the Pure Land of Non-arising, Will certainly be born in the Land of Peace and Bliss.
If a person has committed many sins and should fall into the hells, Upon merely hearing the name of Amitābha, The raging fires become cool and refreshing.
If one recollects Amitābha Buddha, immeasurable sins will be extinguished; one shall experience incomparable bliss in the present life and will certainly be reborn in the Pure Land hereafter.
At that time, Avalokiteśvara rose from his seat and spoke these verses:
The two Honored Ones are like the rising sun, Able to shatter the darkness of birth and death. They reveal the causes and conditions of the past, Unfailing throughout kalpas.
I recall that in immeasurable kalpas, While on the shore of a remote island, At the time of first generating the resolve, They were always at Potalaka;
In former times, while still within birth and death, [they remained there].
The two Honored Ones act as my parents; Now they abide in pure and impure lands, Assisting one another to transform the world.
At that time, Mahāsthāmaprāpta spoke these verses:
"From the moment I first resolved for enlightenment, I followed the two Honored Ones without ever being parted; Now I hear of our past causes and conditions."
"Knowing that conditions will not cease, when I move even a single foot, may the three evil realms be freed from suffering;
and when I am born in the Pure Land, may he extend his hand to welcome me to the West.
At that time, the King of Sovereign Retention also spoke in verse:
"I was your friend in the past; today I am able to know this. Those who shall hear it in the future will certainly be born in the Pure Land.
At that time, Amitābha Buddha suddenly vanished from view. The great assembly rejoiced, paid their respects, and departed.
The Sutra on the Fundamental Causes and Conditions for the Bodhisattva Avalokiteśvara’s Rebirth in the Pure Land.
